{{Short description|Concept in differential geometry}}
In [[differential geometry]], a field of [[mathematics]], a '''Courant algebroid''' is a vector bundle together with an inner product and a compatible bracket more general than that of a [[Lie algebroid]].

It is named after [[Theodore James Courant|Theodore Courant]], who had implicitly devised in 1990<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Courant |first=Theodore James |date=1990 |title=Dirac manifolds |url=https://www.ams.org/journals/tran/1990-319-02/S0002-9947-1990-0998124-1/ |journal=[[Transactions of the American Mathematical Society]] |language=en |volume=319 |issue=2 |pages=631–661 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9947-1990-0998124-1 |issn=0002-9947}}</ref> the standard prototype of Courant algebroid through his discovery of a skew-symmetric bracket on <math>TM\oplus T^*M</math>, called [[Courant bracket]] today, which fails to satisfy the [[Jacobi identity]]. The general notion of Courant algebroid was introduced by Zhang-Ju Liu, [[Alan Weinstein]] and Ping Xu in their investigation of doubles of [[Lie bialgebroid]]s in 1997.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Liu |first1=Zhang-Ju |last2=Weinstein |first2=Alan |author-link2=Alan Weinstein |last3=Xu |first3=Ping |date=1997-01-01 |title=Manin triples for Lie bialgebroids |url=https://projecteuclid.org/journals/journal-of-differential-geometry/volume-45/issue-3/Manin-triples-for-Lie-bialgebroids/10.4310/jdg/1214459842.full |journal=[[Journal of Differential Geometry]] |volume=45 |issue=3 |arxiv=dg-ga/9508013 |doi=10.4310/jdg/1214459842 |issn=0022-040X}}</ref>

==Definition==
A '''Courant algebroid''' consists of the data a [[vector bundle]] <math>E\to M</math> with a bracket <math>[\cdot,\cdot]:\Gamma E \times \Gamma E \to \Gamma E</math>, a non degenerate fiber-wise inner product <math>\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle: E\times E\to M\times\R</math>, and a bundle map <math>\rho:E\to TM </math> (called anchor) subject to the following axioms:

# Jacobi identity: <math>[\phi, [\chi, \psi]] = [[\phi, \chi], \psi] + [\chi, [\phi, \psi]]</math>
# Leibniz rule: <math>[\phi, f\psi] = \rho(\phi)f\psi +f[\phi, \psi]</math>
# Obstruction to skew-symmetry: <math>[\phi,\psi] + [\psi,\phi] = \tfrac12 D\langle \phi,\psi \rangle</math>
# Invariance of the inner product under the bracket: <math>\rho(\phi)\langle \psi,\chi \rangle= \langle [\phi,\psi],\chi \rangle + \langle \psi, [\phi,\chi] \rangle </math>

where <math>\phi, \chi, \psi</math> are sections of ''<math>E</math>'' and ''<math>f</math>'' is a [[Smoothness|smooth function]] on the base manifold ''<math>M</math>''. The map ''<math>D: \mathcal{C}^\infty(M) \to \Gamma E</math>'' is the composition <math>\kappa^{-1}\rho^T d: \mathcal{C}^\infty(M) \to \Gamma E</math>, with ''<math>d: \mathcal{C}^\infty(M) \to \Omega^1 (M)</math>'' the de Rham differential, <math>\rho^T</math> the dual map of <math>\rho</math>, and ''<math>\kappa</math>'' the isomorphism <math>E \to E^*</math> induced by the inner product.

===Skew-symmetric definition===

An alternative definition can be given to make the bracket [[Bilinear form#Symmetric, skew-symmetric and alternating forms|skew-symmetric]] as

: <math>[[\phi,\psi]]= \tfrac12\big([\phi,\psi]-[\psi,\phi]\big.)</math>

This no longer satisfies the Jacobi identity axiom above. It instead fulfills a homotopic Jacobi identity.

:<math> [[\phi,[[\psi,\chi]]\,]] +\text{cycl.} = DT(\phi,\psi,\chi)</math>

where ''<math>T</math>'' is

: <math>T(\phi,\psi,\chi)=\frac13\langle [\phi,\psi],\chi\rangle +\text{cycl.}</math>

The Leibniz rule and the invariance of the scalar product become modified by the relation <math> [[\phi,\psi]] = [\phi,\psi] -\tfrac12 D\langle \phi,\psi\rangle</math> and the violation of skew-symmetry gets replaced by the axiom 
::<math> \rho\circ D = 0 </math>

The skew-symmetric bracket ''<math>[[\cdot,\cdot]]</math>'' together with the derivation ''<math>D</math>'' and the Jacobiator ''<math>T</math>'' form a [[strongly homotopic Lie algebra]].

==Properties==
The bracket ''<math>[\cdot,\cdot]</math>'' is not skew-symmetric as one can see from the third axiom. Instead it fulfills a certain Jacobi identity (first axiom) and a Leibniz rule (second axiom). From these two axioms one can derive that the anchor map ''<math>\rho</math>'' is a morphism of brackets: 
::<math> \rho[\phi,\psi] = [\rho(\phi),\rho(\psi)] .</math>

The fourth rule is an invariance of the inner product under the bracket. Polarization leads to
::<math> \rho(\phi)\langle \chi,\psi\rangle= \langle [\phi,\chi],\psi\rangle +\langle \chi,[\phi,\psi]\rangle .</math>

==Examples==
An example of the Courant algebroid is given by the [[Dorfman bracket]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Dorfman |first=Irene Ya. |date=1987-11-16 |title=Dirac structures of integrable evolution equations |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/0375960187902015 |journal=[[Physics Letters A]] |volume=125 |issue=5 |pages=240–246 |doi=10.1016/0375-9601(87)90201-5 |bibcode=1987PhLA..125..240D |issn=0375-9601|url-access=subscription }}</ref> on the direct sum <math>TM\oplus T^*M</math> with a twist introduced by Ševera in 1988,<ref>{{cite arXiv |last=Ševera |first=Pavol |title=Letters to Alan Weinstein about Courant algebroids |date=2017-07-05 |class=math.DG |eprint=1707.00265}}</ref> defined as:
::<math> [X+\xi, Y+\eta] := [X,Y]+(\mathcal{L}_X\,\eta -\iota_Y d\xi +\iota_X \iota_Y H)</math>
where ''<math>X,Y</math>'' are vector fields, <math>\xi, \eta</math> are 1-forms and ''<math>H</math>'' is a closed 3-form twisting the bracket. This bracket is used to describe the integrability of [[generalized complex geometry|generalized complex structures]].

A more general example arises from a [[Lie algebroid]] ''<math>A</math>'' whose induced differential on <math>A^*</math> will be written as ''<math>d</math>'' again. Then use the same formula as for the Dorfman bracket with ''<math>H</math>'' an ''A''-3-form closed under ''<math>d</math>''.

Another example of a Courant algebroid is a quadratic Lie algebra, i.e. a Lie algebra with an invariant scalar product. Here the base manifold is just a point and thus the anchor map (and ''<math>D</math>'') are trivial.

The example described in the paper by Weinstein et al. comes from a Lie bialgebroid: if ''<math>A</math>'' is a Lie algebroid (with anchor <math>\rho_A</math> and bracket <math>[.,.]_A</math>), also its dual <math>A^*</math> is a Lie algebroid (inducing the differential <math>d_{A^*}</math> on <math>\wedge^* A</math>) and <math>d_{A^*}[X,Y]_A=[d_{A^*}X,Y]_A+[X,d_{A^*}Y]_A</math> (where on the right-hand side you extend the ''<math>A</math>''-bracket to <math>\wedge^*A</math> using graded Leibniz rule). This notion is symmetric in ''<math>A</math>'' and <math>A^*</math> (see Roytenberg). Here <math>E=A\oplus A^*</math> with anchor <math>\rho(X+\alpha)=\rho_A(X)+\rho_{A^*}(\alpha)</math> and the bracket is the skew-symmetrization of the above in <math>X</math> and ''<math>\alpha</math>'' (equivalently in ''<math>Y</math>'' and <math>\beta</math>):

:<math>[X+\alpha,Y+\beta]= ([X,Y]_A +\mathcal{L}^{A^*}_{\alpha}Y-\iota_\beta d_{A^*}X) +([\alpha,\beta]_{A^*} +\mathcal{L}^A_X\beta-\iota_Yd_{A}\alpha)</math>.

== Dirac structures ==
{{See also|Dirac structure}}
Given a Courant algebroid with the inner product <math>\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle</math> of split signature (e.g. the standard one <math>TM\oplus T^*M</math>), a [[Dirac structure]] is a maximally isotropic integrable vector subbundle ''<math>L \to M</math>'', i.e.
:<math> \langle L,L\rangle \equiv 0</math>,

:<math> \mathrm{rk}\,L=\tfrac12\mathrm{rk}\,E</math>,

:<math> [\Gamma L,\Gamma L]\subset \Gamma L</math>.

=== Examples ===
As discovered by Courant and parallel by Dorfman, the graph of a 2-form <math>\omega \in \Omega^2(M)</math> is maximally isotropic and moreover integrable if and only if <math>d \omega = 0</math>, i.e. the 2-form is closed under the de Rham differential, i.e. is a presymplectic structure.

A second class of examples arises from bivectors <math>\Pi\in\Gamma(\wedge^2 TM)</math> whose graph is maximally isotropic and integrable if and only if <math>[\Pi,\Pi] = 0</math>, i.e. <math>\rho</math> is a [[Poisson manifold|Poisson bivector]] on ''<math>M</math>''.

== Generalized complex structures ==
{{See also|Generalized complex geometry}}
Given a Courant algebroid with inner product of split signature, a generalized complex structure ''<math>L \to M</math>'' is a Dirac structure in the [[complexification|complexified]] Courant algebroid with the additional property 
:<math> L \cap \bar{L} = 0</math>

where <math>\bar{\ }</math> means [[Complex conjugate|complex conjugation]] with respect to the standard complex structure on the complexification.

As studied in detail by Gualtieri,<ref>{{cite arXiv |last=Gualtieri |first=Marco |title=Generalized complex geometry |date=2004-01-18  |eprint=math/0401221 }}</ref> the generalized complex structures permit the study of geometry analogous to [[complex manifold|complex geometry]].

=== Examples ===
Examples are, besides presymplectic and Poisson structures, also the graph of a [[Complex Manifold#Almost complex structures|complex structure]] <math>J: TM \to TM</math>.
